question: Bill Gates's 'five questions' (How to Avoid a Climate Disaster): (a) 'How much space do you need?' (power density / land-use intensity of each way of making electricity) and (b) 'How much power are we talking about?' (the kilowatt-gigawatt-terawatt scale ladder). Gates's book itself is copyrighted (no data taken from it); its power-density table is drawn from Smil, which is not usable (see candidates).

need.question: a
need.need: Power density (W/m2) or land-use intensity (ha/TWh/y or m2/MWh) per electricity source: coal, gas, nuclear, hydro, onshore wind (footprint and spacing), offshore wind, ground PV, rooftop PV, CSP, biomass, geothermal. Median and range from an open-licence producer, with scope stated (direct only, or incl. fuel supply/mining).

need.question: b
need.need: Open, producer-published reference values for the scale ladder: one home (kW), one large power station (GW), one city (GW), the world's electricity demand and total primary energy as average power (TW).

values.location_in_file: article text, methods: 'Integrated Solar PV, i.e. rooftop solar, is assigned an LUIE of zero in this study.'

third_party_flags: S1 File hydro rows (951) are each credited 'International Commission on Large Dams (ICOLD)'; the paper says the dataset 'is compiled from International Commission on Large Dam's (ICOLD) World Register of Dams database'. The World Register of Dams is a subscription database; its terms were not checked. Per-dam rows (with dam names) should not be mirrored or published; the Table 1 aggregate is the authors' own statistic.

Geothermal rows credited 'Bertani (2005) & Global Energy Observatory'; coal, gas, biomass, CSP rows are values taken from other papers (Fthenakis & Kim 2009, NETL 2014, Lilliestam et al. 2021, Ong et al. 2013, Smil 2010/2015 etc.). Facts compiled under the article's CC BY; flag in attribution.
Nuclear and wind direct areas are the authors' own polygons drawn in Google Earth Pro, with EIA generation (public domain).
headline_checks: Table 1 read from the article XML on 2026-10-08: nuclear 7.1, dedicated biomass 58,000 ha/TWh/y; the abstract states the same two numbers ('from nuclear with 7.1 ha/TWh/y to dedicated biomass at 58,000 ha/TWh/y').

Recomputed from S1 File for checking only: Solar PV Total median 1,974.3 (n 94) ~ Table 1 2,000; Wind- (footprint) 129.62 (n 57) ~ 130; Wind+ (spacing) 11,907 ~ 12,000; Geothermal 45.005 (n 26) = 45; Hydro 647 (n 951 vs Table 1 n 952) ~ 650; Solar CSP Direct 1,291.87 (n 101) ~ 1,300; Biomass Total 58,405.5 (n 14) ~ 58,000; NG- Indirect 357.2 (n 18 vs 17) vs 410; NG+ 1,854 (n 4) ~ 1,900; Nuclear Direct 6.53 (n 65) + Indirect 0.06 vs 7.1; Coal Total 1,309 (n 20) vs 1,000 (n 30). Coal, gas and nuclear in Table 1 combine direct and indirect rows in ways the file does not show, and residue biomass (n 4) is not in the file, so only Table 1 is publishable as is.

For comparison only (not to publish without a recorded transformation): 1 ha/TWh/y corresponds to 11,408 W/m2, so ground PV 2,000 ha/TWh/y = 5.7 W/m2, wind spacing 12,000 = 0.95 W/m2, wind footprint 130 = 88 W/m2, nuclear 7.1 = 1,607 W/m2, coal 1,000 = 11.4 W/m2, dedicated biomass 58,000 = 0.20 W/m2.
caveats: Unit is hectares occupied per terawatt-hour generated in a year (ha/TWh/y); Table 1 'IQR' is the width (Q3 minus Q1), not the two quartiles. Quartile bounds exist only by recomputing from S1 File, which the tree may not do.

Scope: includes fuel-supply land (mining, processing, transport) for coal, gas, nuclear and dedicated biomass; excludes land to mine materials for panels, turbines and plants, transmission corridors, offshore areas and underground impacts. No offshore wind value. Rooftop PV is zero by assumption.
Nuclear, wind and ground PV use US facilities only; coal US and Canada; hydro 80 countries. Hydro excludes run-of-river (paper cites about 10 ha/TWh/y from Fthenakis & Kim, not in Table 1).
Wind and gas each have two values (footprint vs spacing) that differ ~90-fold for wind; both must be shown with the definition.
candidates.recommendation: Register as the primary source for question (a): new source lovering-2022 (open, CC BY 4.0), artifact = article JATS XML (Table 1 parsed strictly, with a check that the abstract still says 7.1 and 58,000). Publish median and IQR width per source in the producer's unit (ha/TWh/y); any W/m2 view must be a pipeline transformation recorded as a processing step. Register S1 File only as a checking artifact with mirror_raw: false because of the ICOLD-derived per-dam rows. Pair with Nøland 2022 for offshore wind and rooftop PV.

values.statistic: median (mean 7.29, n 20); utility-scale PV 5.84 (n 3), residential PV 6.62 (n 4), CSP 9.70 (n 2)

third_party_flags: Every value is taken from a third-party publication (177 densities from the literature, including Smil 1983/2010, NREL, EIA, IRENA, Pimentel), then normalised with US capacity factors and efficiencies (sheet 'Assumptions', Hankey et al. 2017 = EIA). Facts, but the compilation credit must name the authors.
headline_checks: Results summary read on 2026-10-08: gas 482.10 > nuclear 240.81 > oil 194.61 > coal 135.10 > solar 6.63 > geothermal 2.24 > wind 1.84 > hydro 0.135 > biomass 0.081 W/m2 — matches the abstract claim that gas and solar have the highest median density among non-renewable and renewable systems.
caveats: Method weakness: many fossil rows are computed from a fuel's calorific value (MJ/kg, Mcal/m3) with factors 'Infrastructure: N', not from occupied land, e.g. 24 of 34 coal rows. Those are not land-use measurements; coal's 135 W/m2 is far above Lovering's 11 W/m2 incl. mining.
US-centric, small n per sub-type (offshore 3, CSP 2), several values more than 40 years old.

The supplementary file URLs were found on Elsevier's CDN (ars.els-cdn.com answered 200) while the article page itself was blocked; a person should confirm on the article page that mmc1/mmc2 are the article's supplementary files and record them with envdash snapshot add.
candidates.recommendation: Do not use as the headline source because of the calorific-value method for fossil fuels. Keep as a reference only; its biomass value reaches the site through Nøland 2022 anyway.
